items.title: Number of High-Intent Home Shoppers Dropped to a New Low Last Quarter as Stubborn Mortgage Rates Stymied Demand
items.description: Number of High-Intent Home Shoppers Dropped to a New Low Last Quarter as Stubborn Mortgage Rates Stymied Demand Buffalo, Hartford, Providence and San Francisco remain the most competitive markets Written by Treh Manhertz on November 23, 2026 The number of engaged home shoppers — Zillow users who save or share a for-sale listing — fell 4.8% from a year earlier to 3.5 per listing in the third quarter of 2026, the lowest level since Zillow began tracking the metric in 2023. Engaged shoppers per listing declined from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, led by Seattle, Washington, D.C. and Louisville. Four of the six major markets where engagement increased were in Florida. Luxury homes are drawing more than twice as many engaged shoppers per listing as starter homes. Home-buying demand last quarter hit the lowest level Zillow has tracked. Mortgage rates rose from July through September, leaving fewer serious shoppers in the market. The long-running inventory recovery is also spreading that dwindling demand across more homes. The number of engaged home shoppers per listing fell to 3.5 nationally in the third quarter of 2026. An engaged shopper is defined as a Zillow user who saved or shared a for-sale listing, signaling real interest beyond casual browsing. Agent activity is excluded from this analysis. The 3.5 engaged shoppers per listing last quarter is down 4.8% from a year earlier and the lowest level for any quarter since Zillow began tracking the metric in the second half of 2023. The pullback was widespread, with engagement down from last year in 44 of the 50 largest metro areas, although major Florida markets were an exception. Higher mortgage costs are the most likely driver of the drop in demand. Mortgage rates averaged 6.43% in Freddie Mac’s July 2 Primary Mortgage Market Survey , and rose to 7.28% by October 1. That jump in rates is enough to increase the monthly mortgage payment on a $400,000 home by nearly $200, from $2,008 to $2,189 (assuming a 20% down payment). Typical mortgage costs rose year over year in August, September and October, ending a 10-month streak of annual declines. Inventory keeps growing as shoppers pull back, helping bring down the number of engaged shoppers per listing. As of October, for-sale inventory has risen on an annual basis for 35 consecutive months, though it remains 14.4% below pre-pandemic norms. New listings have been a mixed bag, up on a year-over-year basis in just six of the past 12 months, suggesting the inventory buildup is more a result of homes staying on the market longer than a surge of new sellers. Nearly every major metro saw home shoppers pull back The pullback was widespread. Seattle saw the steepest drop in engaged shoppers per listing, down 17.1% from a year earlier. Washington, D.C. (-15.5%), Louisville (-14.3%), Salt Lake City (-13.7%) and Minneapolis (-13.4%) followed. Only six large metros posted gains, and four of them are in Florida: Jacksonville (+12.2%), Miami (+8.7%), Tampa (+4.2%) and Orlando (+0.8%). San Francisco (+5.1%) and Birmingham (+0.9%) were the others. Buffalo (6.7 engaged shoppers per listing), Hartford (6.2), Providence (6.1), San Francisco (6) and San Diego (5.2) had the most engagement last quarter. Despite its 8.7% year-over-year bounceback, Miami was one of the coolest markets with just 1.9 engaged shoppers per listing. Only Houston (1.6) had fewer. Luxury engagement holds steady while starter-home interest slides Luxury listings — homes among the top 5% most valuable in a given metro — typically drew 6.4 engaged shoppers last quarter, flat from a year earlier. Starter homes — homes in the 5th to 35th percentile of home values in a given metro — typically drew 2.9 engaged shoppers, down 8.2% year over year. This reflects the “K-shaped” housing market that has emerged. Economic headwinds such as slower hiring and rising inflation are prompting many households to delay major financial commitments like a home purchase. Higher-income households are in a different position. Stock market gains have boosted buying power, while higher mortgage rates have little impact on those who can make an all-cash purchase. Rental market is seeing spillover demand With for-sale demand waning, many would-be buyers appear to be turning to rentals instead. Nationally, rental demand is up 22.1% from a year earlier, according to Zillow’s October Rental Market Report . Demand for single-family rentals is up 24.3%, roughly double the 12.1% rise for apartments. The typical single-family rent is $2,243 a month, about $360 less than the monthly cost of owning a single-family home with 20% down. items.title: Flat Conditions for Built-to-Rent Construction
items.description: Flat Conditions for Built-to-Rent Construction November 23, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments Single-family built-for-rent (SFBFR, or built-to-rent (BTR)) construction was flat for the third quarter of 2026, just prior to enactment of legislation that, fortunately, did not include harmful financing rules for BTR housing. A rebound for the sector may be in store given priced-out homebuyers and certainty regarding financing rules. According to NAHB’s analysis of data from the Census Bureau’s Quarterly Starts and Completions by Purpose and Design , there were approximately 19,000 single-family built-for-rent ( SFBFR ) starts during the third quarter of 2026. This is up 6% from the third quarter of 2025 (18,000). Over the last four quarters, 69,000 such homes began construction, which is flat from the estimated BTR starts for the prior four quarter period (also 69,000). The BTR market is a source of inventory amid challenges regarding housing affordability and down payment requirements in the for-sale market, particularly during a period when a growing number of people want more space and a single-family structure. Single-family built-for-rent construction differs in structural characteristics compared to other newly-built single-family homes, particularly with respect to home size. Given the relatively small size of this market segment, the quarter-to-quarter movements typically are not statistically significant. The current four-quarter moving average of market share (just above 7%) is nonetheless higher than the historical average of 2.7% (1992-2012). Importantly, as measured for this analysis, the estimates noted above include only homes built and held by the builder for rental purposes. The estimates exclude homes that are sold to another party for rental purposes, which NAHB estimates may represent another three to five percent of single-family starts based on industry surveys. The Census data note an elevated share of single-family homes built as condos (non-fee simple), with this share averaging about 3% over recent quarters. Some, but certainly not all, of these homes will be used for rental purposes. Additionally, it is theoretically possible that some single-family built-for-rent units are being counted in multifamily starts, as a form of “horizontal multifamily,” given that these units are often built on a single plat of land. However, spot checks by NAHB with permitting offices continue to indicate no evidence of this data issue occurring. With the onset of the Great Recession and declines in the homeownership rate , the share of built-for-rent homes increased in the years after the recession. While the market share of SFBFR homes is small, it has clearly expanded. items.title: $500M Data Center Debt Auction Fizzles, Leaving Dutch Bank To Shop For Buyers
items.description: An auction for $500M worth of data center debt stumbled out of the gate, and the lender is now at the door of buyers looking to make a deal. ING Bank Lackluster demand for the $500M worth of debt, including some backing high-profile data center projects in the U.S., led Dutch bank ING to abandon a so-called bids-wanted-in-competition process and turn to closing individual deals to clear the debt, Bloomberg reported Friday. The loans for sale are complicated and not easy to trade, and some buyers needed more time to evaluate the assets while ING was examining whether any of the offers it received through the bidding process were acceptable, Bloomberg reported, citing multiple anonymous sources who asked not to be identified to discuss private information. ING declined to comment when reached by Bisnow on Monday. The auction included a $25M piece of debt backing a massive joint venture called Project Jupiter from OpenAI and Oracle in New Mexico, but bids for the debt came in too low, sources told Bloomberg. There are other signs that investors have grown skeptical about Project Jupiter's scope and timeline. HSBC sold $300M in data center construction debt tied to Project Jupiter at less than 90 cents on the dollar earlier this month. The financing, part of an $18B package assembled by 20 banks, is backing a project that has faced widening community pushback and permitting hurdles. In September, Oracle sent a force majeure notice to the project's developer, Blue Owl Capital -owned Stack Infrastructure , looking to delay some rent payments due to setbacks at the project site. HSBC sold its $300M chunk immediately after the force majeure notice was sent, according to Bloomberg. ING was first reported to be shopping the $500M debt package earlier this month. The debt, a package of 12 loans, is also tied to data centers being developed by major operators like Vantage and CyrusOne . Some of the debt is associated with developments in Stargate , the sprawling Texas development project launched from the White House in January 2025. The attempted auction was reportedly the first to involve a portfolio made up solely of data center debt, and it comes as the broader artificial intelligence market tries to push through a sell-off and the sector-shaking news that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had several affairs, including with a suspected Chinese spy. Huang was ousted from the company he founded earlier this month only to be renamed to the top post Monday, sending the stock soaring more than 30%, although still down 20% from a month ago. The Magnificent 7 index, which tracks the seven mega-cap technology stocks, was up 8% on the news of Huang’s return in early trading Monday but remains down more than 4% over the last 30 days. Investors are beginning to question the run-up in tech stocks as the firms pour billions of dollars into the build-out of infrastructure to support as-yet-unproven AI systems. Anthropic , the maker of the Claude chatbot and a leading name in AI, went public last week at a valuation above $2T, but the stock was left out of the exuberance of Huang’s return to the fold Monday, with shares down more than 15% from the stock’s debut last week. items.title: Washington state regulator issues temporary stop on new business for Directors Mortgage
items.description: The Washington Department of Financial Institutions (DFI) has ordered Directors Mortgage to temporarily stop taking on new business in the state, including the origination of loans for Washington residents or for properties located in the state, citing exam interference and concerns about the company’s finances. According to the DFI’s order, examiners who conducted an on-site review at the Oregon-based lender’s main office from Nov. 17 to Nov. 19 were not provided requested information and records. During that period, the department served a subpoena on the company’s CEO and owner to obtain the production of original books, accounts, papers, records and files. The department also said it obtained information during the examination indicating that the company was not meeting its financial obligations to employees or third-party vendors. “Respondent’s failure to comply with the Department’s examination authority and Respondent’s current financial condition pose a serious risk of injury to the public,” the order states. A representative of Directors Mortgage did not immediately respond to HousingWire ’s request for comment. The emergency order, signed on Friday by Brian J. Guerard, Washington DFI’s acting director, requires Directors Mortgage to deliver detailed financial information, including balance sheets and bank account data, and to fully respond to the department’s subpoena. The order also directs the company to satisfy outstanding financial obligations. Under Washington law, companies may contest such orders in an administrative hearing. If a respondent does not seek a hearing, the order becomes permanent when DFI issues a final order. Directors Mortgage, founded in 1998 by president and CEO Mark J. Hanna and headquartered in Oregon, has originated about $235 million in mortgages year to date, according to InGenius . The company had roughly 40 loan officers and nine active branches as of Monday, per data from the Nationwide Multistate Licensing System . Washington’s DFI has been active recently regarding mortgage enforcement. Newrez recently agreed to pay roughly $3 million and implement wide-ranging mortgage servicing changes to resolve allegations by the department that it engaged in unfair or deceptive acts or practices. Earlier this year, Washington state regulators issued a $75,000 fine and a $3,000 investigation fee against West Capital Lending , alleging multiple violations of the state's consumer loan act. The company was accused of allowing unlicensed individuals to conduct mortgage-related activities and of failing to meet certain disclosure and reporting requirements. Per the agreement, WCL did not admit to the allegations nor any wrongdoing. Meanwhile, Rocket Mortgage and Mr. Cooper Group recently agreed to pay a combined $6.75 million to the New York State Department of Financial Services to resolve allegations of cybersecurity violations tied to data protection, risk assessments and incident reporting. items.title: The Geography of the Crowded Nest: Where Adults Are Living with Their Parents
items.description: The Geography of the Crowded Nest: Where Adults Are Living with Their Parents By Hannah Jones Nov 23, 2026 Key Takeaways A record 25.2 million adults under 35 live with their parents in 2025 — more than at any point on record, including the pandemic peak. At 33.0%, the share of young adults living at home is just below the all-time high of 33.6% set in 2020. Regionally, co-residence rates are highest in the Northeast, with 36.9% of 18-34 year-olds living with their parents, well-above the national rate. All other regions saw rates clustered just below the national norm. Though the Northeast sees the highest rate of co-residence, it is the only region that has seen significant improvement, with the lowest rate of adults at home since 2010. New York leads all major metros with 41.3% of young adults (18-34) living at home. Las Vegas and San Francisco have seen the sharpest post-pandemic deterioration, with co-residence rates rising more than 4 percentage points since the pandemic period. Nationally, a record-breaking 25.2 million adults under 35 are still under their parent’s roof , translating to roughly 1 in 3 young adults. The national figure masks a regional divide. In the Northeast, 36.9% of young adults live at home, the highest share of any region, followed by the West (32.4%), the South (32.3%) and the Midwest (31.7%). While the Northeast has seen modest improvement from its peak, the other three regions remain at or above pandemic-era highs. Home prices have risen sharply in every region since the pandemic, but the Northeast (+50.8%) and Midwest (+48.4%) have seen the steepest increases, with the West (+38.5%) and South (+34.8%) not far behind. With all four regions seeing price growth of at least 35% above pre-pandemic levels, the basic arithmetic of independent living has become harder to clear, and elevated rents have compounded the pressure for those not yet positioned to buy. For many young adults, staying home has become less a choice than a default, a way to keep options open until the gap between their incomes and housing costs narrows. Highest Rates, But Finally Easing: The Northeast Exception Over the last 25 years, the Northeast has seen an average 37.1% of young adults living at home, well above the national average of 30.2% in the same 25-year span. The other regions see lower rates, with 29.4% of young adults at home in the Midwest, and 28.5% in each the South and West. In 2025, the Northeast saw a co-residence rate of 36.9% for 18-34 year-olds. items.title: Mount Street Establishes New Dallas Hub, Buys $1.4B Servicing Business
items.description: London-based finance firm Mount Street Group has hired a team of seasoned primary and special servicing professionals to establish a Dallas hub. The expansion deal will add almost $1.4B of assets to its approximately $30B U.S. servicing book, according to an announcement on Monday . The group, led by former Credit Suisse credit chief Paul Smyth, will oversee the firm’s U.S. securitized products, collateralized loan obligation and special servicing business. Wikimedia Commons/Mx. Granger Mount Street Group's London headquarters at 100 Wood St. “The securitized products and special servicing markets require experience, judgment and a disciplined approach to execution,” Smyth, who was named managing director and head of securitized products in the U.S., said in a statement. “Mount Street’s platform gives us the ability to bring those capabilities to clients at greater scale, supported by a strong global infrastructure and a clear commitment to growth in the U.S. market." The team is made up of executives from Broadsword Investors, co-founded by Smyth, and Goldersun Loan Servicing, both Dallas-based firms. The servicing book was acquired from Goldersun, according to a Mount Street spokesperson. Throughout his 40-year career, Smyth has managed more than $55B in loan resolutions. He served as Credit Suisse ’s global chief credit officer and president of Greystone ’s special servicing portfolio before starting his own specialty finance firm. Broadsword was founded alongside Cary Williams, who will also join Mount Street, focusing on new client initiatives and asset management. Mount Street’s new team also includes Joe Beggins, who was CEO of General Electric Capital Loan Services and GEMSA Loan Services, the subsequent commercial mortgage servicing joint venture between GE and CBRE . Beggins has held leadership positions at other CRE firms since, including managing member of Goldersun. He will oversee asset management and process enhancements for investors at Mount Street. Goldersun CEO Terry Clay will move to Mount Street, where he will serve as head of the surveillance and reporting team. He previously worked at Hudson Advisors. John Roach, who worked with Smyth at other companies, including Greystone, will lead the Dallas team's primary servicing and CLO operations components. In a statement, Rawle Howard, head of Mount Street USA, said the addition of the new team “marks a meaningful acceleration of Mount Street’s U.S. growth strategy.” “Their market credibility, technical expertise and deep experience across securitized products, B-Piece investing, CMBS, special servicing and asset management are highly complementary to our existing platform and will immediately enhance the depth of service we can provide to clients,” Howard said. “This transaction is not just about adding scale; it is about adding the right people, capabilities and leadership to support the next phase of our U.S. growth.” Founded in 2013, Mount Street has more than €163B of assets under administration and €31.9B in assets under valuation, or roughly $177.5B and $34.7B, respectively. It employs more than 200 people across Europe and the U.S. The global third-party loan servicing and credit management business established its North American branch in 2017. Mount Street USA is headquartered in Atlanta. items.title: FHA’s reverse mortgage book faces headwinds from home prices, fewer payoffs
items.description: The Federal Housing Administration ’s fiscal year 2026 actuarial report to Congress says the Home Equity Conversion Mortgage ( HECM ) reverse mortgage portfolio remains a small but volatile slice of the FHA's Mutual Mortgage Insurance Fund, showing that its stand-alone capital ratio dropped significantly in the wake of lower endorsement numbers over the past year. The report , released Nov. 16, found that the MMI Fund's overall capital ratio dropped slightly during the year ending Sept. 30, moving from 11.47% last year to 10.29% this year. The current figure, however, is roughly five times higher than fund's statutory minimum requirement of 2%. Looking exclusively at the HECM portfolio, the capital ratio was down significantly from 24.06% in FY 2025 to 5.43% in FY 2026. The FHA attributed this decline mainly to macroeconomic dynamics and program-specific cash flows. HECM remains profitable but capital buffer tightens The reverse mortgage portfolio, which accounts for less than 4% of the fund's insurance in force, is “much more sensitive to home prices,” the report explained. Slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts have increased projected losses for the HECM program. In addition, loan payoffs — which represent more favorable recovery outcomes than other disposition methods like foreclosures — have become less common and have pushed losses higher. The agency also noted that the HECM program “spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.” These claims, which are generated when FHA acquires loans that hit the 98% maximum claim amount threshold, are a known driver of volatility in the HECM book. They remain a key cost to monitor for reverse mortgage issuers and servicers . While the federally insured reverse mortgage portfolio is still in the black, the takeaway from the report is that its capital support can change rapidly due to shifts in home price appreciation, payoff behaviors and the frequency of assignment claims. These factors drive FHA policy decisions, as well as Ginnie Mae execution in the HECM Mortgage-Backed Securities ( HMBS ) market. HECM volume falls again, proprietary loans fill the gap The report illustrates that FHA-insured options remain central to the wider reverse mortgage market, even as volumes edge lower. In FY 2026, FHA insured 24,162 HECMs representing a maximum claim amount (MCA) of $12.81 billion. Endorsements were down about 14% from the 28,149 HECMs endorsed in FY 2025. MCA volume also fell from about $15.5 billion in 2025 to roughly $13.5 billion in 2026. But even with that pullback, the HECM program “remains a large part of the market,” according to the report. Historic data reinforces the sector’s structural shift. HECM endorsements peaked above 110,000 in 2009 with roughly $30.5 billion in MCA. Volumes have trended lower for more than a decade, with visible rebounds in 2020–2022 during a period of low interest rates and high home price growth. But higher rates and slower price growth since 2023 have softened demand. To fill the gap, lenders are focusing on proprietary reverse mortgages through their retail, wholesale and correspondent channels. The wider availability of these products has propelled a shift in market share as private-label loans accounted for more than 60% of reverse mortgage volume in September, according to New View Advisors . "I think that product diversity is great because we're able to serve more clients that the FHA product wouldn't handle," Jesse Allen , president of 55+ lending at Rate , told HousingWire 's Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD) at this month's National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Meeting & Expo. He said these may be " mass affluent clients who have home values of $2 million or $3 million, and they really want to tap their equity without the debt service to achieve their goals," but they can also be clients who don't fit the HECM qualification requirements and are using reverse mortgage proceeds to consolidate debt. "This is another regulatory guideline NRMLA has advocated for. 'Hey, we're paying off consumer debts. Let's not count that toward the the qualification process.' Proprietary allows us to do that and HECM does not," Allen said. Portfolio characteristics, sensitivity to home prices FHA's FY 2026 report includes a dedicated HECM chapter that details borrower profiles and loan features. These include HECM loan purposes (such as home purchases versus refinancing of existing debt), payment plan options, interest rate types, borrower ages and maximum claim amounts and initial draws by recent borrower cohorts. The agency emphasizes that its actuaries model HECM cash flows separately from forward mortgages and explicitly stress-test the reverse portfolio under varying home price appreciation scenarios. Home price appreciation assumptions affect multiple levers across the program — including the available equity at the end of the loan, the size of recoveries through property sales and the loss severity tied to claims. Indirectly, home price growth can also impact payoff incentives. The report notes that waning price growth in 2026 had an “outsized negative impact” on HECM capital compared with forward mortgages. This underscores why even modest regional or national home price corrections are more consequential for HMBS investors and issuers than for traditional mortgage-backed securities . The stand-alone capital ratio of 5.43% for the HECM portfolio suggests that FHA still has room to absorb stress, but far less cushion than in the prior three years when the ratio ranged between roughly 16% and 25%. It also may create more difficulty for industry advocates in their push to reduce upfront mortgage insurance premiums. items.title: New York Governor signs new rules for private listings into law, Compass praises it
items.description: New York’s governor has joined the growing lists of state lawmakers enacting laws to govern the use of private listing networks. On Friday, Governor Kathy Hochul signed Senate Bill S10274, also known as the “ Fair and Transparent Real Estate Listings Act ,” into law, just seven days after it was delivered to her desk. The legislation was first introduced in mid-March before going on to pass the Assembly in late May and the state Senate on June 1, 2026. The law requires residential listings to be publicly advertised or marketed on platforms that are accessible to the general public. According to the law, this means that the publication, platform or website the listing is advertised on does not require payment or for the consumer to work with a certain brokerage or agent in order to view the property information. Additionally, the law specifies that any licensed real estate broker or agent working with a buyer without limitation to a particular brokerage, franchise, or select group of licensees should also be able to view information about the listing. Here's how it will impact real estate professionals and brokerages: Despite this emphasis on ensuring listing information is easily accessible, the law does note that sellers who sign a state-provided standardized disclosure form explaining the risks and tradeoffs associated with non-public marketing, may withhold their listing from public marketing. In the disclosure included in the text of the law, sellers must acknowledge that their property “may not be marketed or distributed outside the real estate brokerage that the listing agent is associated with through mass-marketing channels,” and that due to this, the seller understands that the reduced exposure of the property may lead to a reduction in the number of offers they receive, potentially negatively impacting their ability to sell the house. Those who break this law can be fined up to $5,000. In addition, under the law, the Department of State may suspend or revoke a real estate professional’s license. The law is set to go into effect in late May 2027. Brokerage executives praise law Bess Freedman, the CEO of New York City-based Brown Harris Stevens , a RealTrends Verified brokerage, is celebrating the passage of the law. “Buying a home shouldn’t depend on who you know or which brokerage you work with. I’m proud that New York is taking on private listing networks and making public marketing the standard,” Freedman wrote in an emailed statement. “Buyers deserve to see what’s available and choose who represents them. Sellers deserve the chance to reach the widest possible audience, and those who want privacy — a choice that has always existed — can still choose it with a clear understanding of what they may give up.” In addition to Freedman, Caroline Burton , the general manager of StreetEasy , which is owned by Zillow , is also applauding the news and thanking the state legislature for “putting consumers first.” “When homes are kept out of public view, New Yorkers lose out, especially in a market where homes for sale are already scarce,” Burton wrote in an emailed statement. “Finding a home in the most challenging market shouldn’t depend on privilege, who you know or who you work with. In one of the biggest decisions in a person’s life, New Yorkers deserve an open and transparent marketplace so they can make an informed choice. This is a win for all buyers, sellers, and the agents who serve them.” Compass excited about homeowner choice Beyond these two firms, which had been vocal proponents of listing transparency, Compass International Holdings, which has been promoting its three-phased marketing plan , which includes a private listing phase , is also praising the enacting of the law . A Compass spokesperson told HousingWire that the new law “preserves homeowners’ right to choose how they market their homes,” which includes marketing the property through Compass's See It First initiative. Compass launched See It First in September . The company said it is intended to expand inventory visibility for buyers, allow sellers to “test and learn ” without public days on market and provide agents with an additional marketing lever. “See It First early access homes comply with the new law and continue to give sellers flexibility in how and when they bring their homes to market,” a Compass spokesperson told HousingWire via email. Similarly, the New York State Association of Realtors (NYSAR) said in a statement that the "legislation strikes an appropriate balance between promoting transparency and protecting consumer choice by preserving the ability of property owners to determine how their properties are marketed." "This new law helps ensure that property owners are fully informed of the potential consequences of limiting the public marketing of their properties, including the possibility of reduced exposure to prospective buyers or tenants," the statement read. Other states weigh in on private listings In enacting this law, New York is joining Connecticut , Wisconsin and Washington in creating a law governing the public marketing of residential properties. New York’s law is similar to the ones passed in Connecticut and Wisconsin, both of which provide sellers the ability to opt-out of public marketing with a signed disclosure. The Washington law, however, does not include a pathway for sellers to opt-out of public marketing besides a health or safety concern. These laws are currently in effect in Connecticut and Wisconsin, with Washington's law slated to go into effect on Jan. 1, 2027. Related More: Brown Harris Stevens Clear Cooperation Co Compass

items.title: CenterSquare sells Kennesaw multifamily community
items.description: CenterSquare sells Kennesaw multifamily community by John Yellig November 23, 2026 The 1997-vintage community mostly offers larger two- and three-bedroom apartments compared to newer developments, which have higher concentrations of one-bedroom units. Via CenterSquare. Philadelphia-based CenterSquare sold the Mill at Chastain, a 240-unit apartment community in Kennesaw. Financial details were not disclosed, but Cobb County tax records show the property last changed hands for approximately $42.6 million on Sept. 29 between seller East Inwood Chastain LLC and buyer Mainstay Townpark LLC. Located on the southeast corner of George Busbeen Parkway and Chastain Road, the 1997-vintage community mostly offers larger two- and three-bedroom apartments compared to newer developments, which have higher concentrations of one-bedroom units, CenterSquare said. The real estate investment firm purchased the property in November 2019 and instituted its “core-plus” business plan, which upgraded select unit interiors for a portion of the property with new faux hardwood flooring, stainless-steel appliances, resurfaced granite countertops, subway tile backsplashes, lighting fixtures and cabinet hardware. The strategy provided the buyers with a value-add opportunity, as 65% of the units had not undergone the improvements, CenterSquare said. “The disposition of the Mill at Chastain marks the successful execution of our core-plus business plan on behalf of one of our long-standing separate account relationships,” said Chris Picyk of CenterSquare’s private real estate team. “We are proud to have operated through the market volatility that took place during the hold period to deliver results for our client.” Read More Related to This Post Toll Brothers begins developing Johns Creek townhome project, Jardin Heights Portman kicks off construction of Brookside Village mixed-use community in Alpharetta Parkland Communities secures $50M development financing, begins Highland Brook in Dacula Ashton Woods names Nicholas Czar SVP of sales Traton Homes begins selling at Flowery Branch townhome community Larkspur Atlanta’s housing market is entering a new phase. items.title: Mountain View Hotel Refinanced with New Loan for $77M
items.description: Mountain View Hotel Refinanced with New Loan for $77M Broadreach Capital Partners has obtained a $77 million refi loan for The Ameswell Hotel, a 255-key, fee-simple luxury hotel located at 800 Moffett Blvd. in Mountain View. Developed by Broadreach from the ground up and opened in 2021, The Ameswell Hotel is a five-story independent luxury hotel offering approximately 24,000 square feet of indoor and outdoor meeting and event space, anchored by an infinity ballroom. The property features three distinct food and beverage concepts, including a signature California cuisine restaurant, a quick-and-casual café and an outdoor wine bar and pool venue. Guestrooms feature floor-to-ceiling windows, premium bedding and a curated art program. Additional amenities include a fitness center, a heated outdoor pool, electric vehicle charging and pet-friendly accommodations. The Ameswell Hotel sits within Silicon Valley's premier corporate corridor, approximately one mile from the Googleplex, Alphabet's global headquarters, and near other major technology employers. It is part of a larger mixed-use campus that includes an adjacent 222,000-square-foot Class A+ office building leased to Alphabet. items.title: Martin Commercial Properties Lands $15M in Construction Money for Phoenix Development
items.description: Martin Commercial Properties Lands $15M in Construction Money for Phoenix Development Martin Commercial Properties' has secured $15 million in construction financing for the ground-up development of a 102,302-square-foot Class A flex industrial project in Phoenix, AZ. The project consists of two buildings with units ranging in size from 3,300 to 26,700 square feet. Martin, a full-service commercial real estate and construction firm, will serve as an anchor tenant in the development, establishing its regional headquarters within the building to support the firm’s expanding operations and continued growth in the market. Located in Phoenix's Deer Valley industrial submarket along the north I-17 corridor, the development is positioned to serve the growing network of suppliers and service businesses supporting Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company’s expanding Arizona operations, covering over 2,000 acres and estimated to total around $265 billion. Anna Siradze, Kim Bishop, Will Hainlen and Lauren Maehler led a Talonvest Capital team that arranged the five-year loan, which includes 36 months of interest-only payments, allowing the borrower to complete construction and pursue lease-up before amortization begins. The loan transitions to a 25-year amortization schedule following the interest-only period and includes a declining sliding scale prepayment penalty. items.title: Single-Family Home Size Rising
items.description: Single-Family Home Size Rising November 23, 2026 Robert Dietz No Comments New single-family home size had been falling since 2015 in response to declining affordability conditions. An exception occurred in 2021, when new home size increased as interest rates reached historic lows. However, as mortgage interest rates increased in 2022 and 2023 and affordability worsened, demand shifted back toward smaller homes. Now, this trend appears to be reversing again as entry-level construction has been weak and construction of larger homes have outperformed the overall market. According to third quarter 2026 data from the Census Quarterly Starts and Completions by Purpose and Design and NAHB analysis, median single-family square floor area was 2,164 square feet, down just a little from the prior quarter. Average (mean) square footage for new single-family homes increased to 2,455 square feet, a small increase year-over-year. On a one-year moving average basis, the average size of a new single-family home increased slightly to 2,433 square feet, while the median size was flat at 2,182. Since 2024 home size has trended higher as the upper end of the housing market has fared better than the entry level. items.title: What's driving seller confidence in 2026
items.description: What's driving seller confidence in 2026 by Elizabeth Kanzeg Rowland November 23, 2026 Sellers put in the research to understand pricing and mortgage rates, leading to higher levels of confidence in the selling process. Uncertain rate outlooks and affordability concerns failed to dampen seller confidence in 2026, according to a new Ipsos study commissioned by Century 21 Real Estate. The group's Home Seller Confidence Report revealed high levels of confidence as sellers balance optimal pricing with the emotional drivers behind a move. Over 1,000 Americans over the age of 21 who were current, prospective or recent home sellers were interviewed for the study. So what's driving the trend? Sellers who prioritize strategy, researchers noted. Secure sellers Sellers have few qualms about selling in today's market conditions. Among homeowners planning to sell within 12 months, 75% believe now is the right time to move. So do 82% of those whose homes were already listed. Seller confidence may be age-dependent, researchers found. A substantial 83% of sellers aged 21 to 34 expressed confidence that now is the right time to sell. Meanwhile, sellers aged 35 to 54 and sellers aged 55-plus reported confidence at rates of 78% and 58%, respectively. What's moving movers? Mortgage rates influenced sellers' actions, but personal incentives drove decisions too. Of sellers interviewed, 86% said their mortgage rate was slightly, moderately, very or extremely influential on the timing of their move. Giving up an auspicious mortgage rate created a pain point for many sellers, with 63% of sellers with a mortgage rate below 5% stating that giving up their rate was emotionally difficult and 54% of all sellers agreeing that giving up their rate was harder than leaving their home. Around 19% of sellers listed mortgage rates as their top reason for moving. But personal reasons were given more often, like change of scenery (27%), finding their next home (25%), a personal life event (22%) and feeling emotionally ready (21%). “Mortgage rates are a big part of the housing conversation, but people don't make decisions about their homes based on rates alone,” said Mike Miedler, president and CEO of Century 21 Real Estate. “New jobs, growing families and other life changes still motivate people to move. Sellers aren't waiting for perfect conditions, but they are approaching that decision with more thought and preparation. They want to understand what their home is worth and how quickly it could sell so they can move forward with confidence.” The pricing problem Many sellers expressed concern over getting the best possible price for their home. This priority became especially pronounced with older sellers. Almost half (47%) of sellers 55-plus listed getting the highest possible sales price as the most important outcome when selling their home. This percentage dropped to 32% for sellers aged 35 to 54 and just 16% for sellers aged 21 to 34. Uncertainty about proper pricing led 58% of all sellers to worry about pricing too high and 27% to worry about pricing too low. Notably, 66% of sellers who sold in the last 24 months seriously reconsidered or changed their asking price before listing — some over four times. Of this cohort, however, 35% never ended up changing the price at all throughout the selling process. Where sellers turn In response to uncertainties like pricing, sellers seek information and guidance. Some look to real estate professionals. The study found that agents have influence over seller pricing decisions. Of sellers who listed with an agent, 59% followed their agent’s pricing recommendation. Other sellers turned to AI, with 54% of sellers saying that AI gave them significantly or somewhat more confidence while selling their home. Around 67% of recent and prospective sellers used AI for tasks like estimating home values, studying local market conditions and researching where to move next. However, many sellers recognized AI's limitations, especially when it came to providing pricing accuracy instead of placating with optimistic estimates. For sellers who compared an agent's recommendation with an AI pricing estimate, 45% reported that their agent was closer to their final sale price. Overall, 46% of those who compared AI and their agent’s pricing advice trusted the agent more, while just 15% trusted AI more. The big picture Strategy and security drive seller choices. Sellers put in the research to understand pricing and mortgage rates, leading to higher levels of confidence in the selling process. “Today's sellers are approaching one of life's biggest financial decisions with more research and intention than ever before,” said Miedler. “They're exploring pricing strategies, evaluating buyer demand and looking for trusted guidance before bringing their homes to market. The sellers who feel most confident are often the ones who have a clear strategy from the start.” Read More Related to This Post October pending home sales could represent bottom of cycle Bleak house: Builder confidence hits 14-year low in November Existing-home sales miss estimates in October Housing affordability improves quarterly, annually in Houston Cotality: Northeast, Midwest drive US home-price growth in September New construction and affordability determine Houston’s hottest communities in Q3 Houston leads the nation in millionaire renter growth Home prices rise in majority of Texas metros but decrease statewide Join the conversation Cancel reply Save my name, email, and website in this browser for the next time I comment.
